title: the Alvar hymns
hook: pilgrims sing ten verses that say they're part of a thousand, and a teacher sets out to find the rest

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Alvar hymns, Periyalvar looked up at God and sang a blessing over him: many years. Who did you bless before asking them for anything? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-five.
screen: `MANY YEARS.` · `TODAY: TEN VERSES, AND A THOUSAND.`

segments.voice: Ten verses, sung by pilgrims at the temple in Kumbakonam. A teacher named Nathamuni hears them and is moved, and then he hears the last verse say these ten are part of a thousand. A thousand? He asks the pilgrims for the rest. They don't have them. He asks everywhere. Nobody does. That, the Sri Vaishnava tradition says, is how a lost Tamil scripture began to come home. Year three met its singer, Nammalvar, the silent boy under the tamarind who answered a riddle. Today, how his songs were nearly lost, and found.
screen: `TEN VERSES AT KUMBAKONAM.` → `TEN OUT OF A THOUSAND?` → `NOBODY HAS THE REST.`

segments.voice: So Nathamuni goes to Tirukkurugur, Nammalvar's town, to the tamarind where the silent boy once sat. Nobody there has the thousand either. But, tradition says, someone gives him a short hymn: the one Madhurakavi, Nammalvar's disciple, sang in praise of his teacher. Recite this, he's told. And he does, over and over, until Nammalvar appears to him and gives back the hymns. Nathamuni sets them to music and teaches them, and his line of teachers would later reach Ramanuja. Notice the key that opened the door. Not a library, and not a clever search. A disciple's song of love for his teacher brought back the teacher's songs. What came back is the Tiruvaymoli, longing set to verse. Sometimes Nammalvar sings as himself. Sometimes he sings as a girl missing her beloved, sending birds as messengers to Vishnu. And sometimes the joy is so full that God and the singer seem to have swallowed each other. Tradition calls this song the Tamil Veda, and Sri Vaishnavas speak of two Vedantas, one in Sanskrit and one in Tamil, read together. So in this telling, a scripture survived because someone heard ten verses, wanted the rest, and kept singing a small hymn of devotion until the rest came.
screen: `TO THE TAMARIND AT TIRUKKURUGUR.` · `A DISCIPLE'S SHORT HYMN.` · `THE SONGS GIVEN BACK.` · `THE TAMIL VEDA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a look back at the Alvar days. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then walk back through them slowly, one breath for each. The king who asked to be a step. Tiruppan's slow look from the feet up. Andal's girls at the door, leaning on the bond. Three lamps in the rain. Periyalvar's many years. And today, ten verses that led to a thousand. Don't weigh them. Notice which one stays a moment longer, and rest there. If you pray, you can offer that moment to God. The bell holds the time.
The Alvar hymns. Today, Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli, lost and found again through a disciple's small hymn, which the tradition calls the Tamil Veda. Today's word.
Your line: the Alvar hymns. Today, ask someone for the rest of something they love, a song, a recipe, a story you've only heard part of. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-five.

screen: `DAY 1225 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: VAISHNAVA THEOLOGY (RAMANUJA'S SRI BHASHYA, SELECTIONS).`

howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas chant Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli in temples and homes alongside the Sanskrit Veda, and remember Nathamuni as the teacher who recovered the hymns.

fork.setup: you're Nathamuni. you've heard ten beautiful verses that say they're part of a thousand, and nobody has the rest. what do you do?
options: go to Nammalvar's town and keep reciting his disciple's hymn.
fork.reveal: tradition says he went to Tirukkurugur and recited Madhurakavi's hymn to Nammalvar until Nammalvar appeared and gave him all the hymns.

original.note: Tamil: the name of Nammalvar's great hymn, which Sri Vaishnavas call the Tamil Veda.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Alvar hymns are folk songs beside the real scripture.
what it means: Sri Vaishnavas call Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli the Tamil Veda and read it with the Sanskrit Upanishads.
what a scholar hears: ubhaya vedanta, the two Vedantas, and the Sri Vaishnava account of the hymns carried from Nathamuni to Ramanuja's school.

notes: Editor: re-angled the lesson. The writer's hook and first half retold Madhurakavi's riddle and the silent boy under the tamarind, already told in full in year three's day 909; the lesson now opens on Nathamuni hearing ten verses and tells the recovery story, pointing back to day 909 for the riddle. The week-end practice now looks back over the actual Alvar days (1220–1225) instead of 'Narada's love that asks nothing', which didn't match day 1219. Carry, word, screens, two match pairs, a myth reveal, the trapdoor and howItsDone ('chief of the Alvars', 'festival of the Tamil Veda') were revised to match.
Nathamuni's recovery: the decad heard at Kumbakonam is traditionally the 'aravamude' decad (5.8); the closing verse's 'of the thousand' is paraphrased. Confirm the reference and wording.

The detail that someone at Tirukkurugur gave Nathamuni Madhurakavi's hymn to recite follows the usual telling (traditionally a disciple in Madhurakavi's line, and a set number of recitations, omitted here); confirm.
'His line of teachers would later reach Ramanuja' (Nathamuni, Yamuna, Ramanuja) follows the Sri Vaishnava guru-parampara; confirm wording.
Tamil spelling திருவாய்மொழி and the stress in 'say' should be checked.
